x.A: Kinesis Data Streams plus Lambda can analyze in real time, but you'd write and maintain the analysis code and also build the delivery to S3.
x.B: Glue is for ETL and isn't an ingestion service for real-time streaming data.
x.C: Firehose ingests the data and delivers it to S3 for the data lake with no administration, and Kinesis Data Analytics analyzes the stream in real time with SQL or Flink. Both are fully managed.
x.D: API Gateway and Lambda can ingest and analyze, but you must build and run the code, and nothing delivers the data to S3 by itself.

x.A: S3 isn't a file system you can mount on EC2 instances natively, and it needs extra tooling that adds latency and complexity.
x.B: An NFS share from the primary instance makes that instance a single point of failure and limits resilience and performance.
x.C: EFS is a shared, resilient file system that every EC2 instance can mount, so all instances see the same images.
x.D: Global Accelerator accelerates traffic to the ALB, but it doesn't cache images, so CloudFront is a better fit for a website with images.
x.E: An Auto Scaling group with at least two instances behind an ALB removes the single instance as a point of failure, and CloudFront caches content at the edge to improve performance.

x.A: A cross-account IAM role in each customer's account with read-only permissions and a trust policy for the company's account gives temporary credentials and no long-term keys. The customer controls and can revoke the access.
x.B: A token vending machine is a custom service to build and secure, and it still requires customers to grant access in some way.
x.C: IAM users with long-term access keys held by the company are riskier, because the keys can leak and must be rotated.
x.D: Cognito users are for application users, not for AWS API access to customer accounts, and the stored password adds risk.

x.A: Peering needs a connection between each pair of VPCs and route updates in each, which doesn't scale across hundreds of accounts.
x.B: Connecting VPCs through the internet with NAT and internet gateways is insecure and complicated.
x.C: A transit gateway in the networking account is a central hub that VPCs attach to. It can be shared with the other accounts, which scales to hundreds of VPCs with the least effort.
x.D: A transit VPC with VPN gateways is a self-managed design that is harder to run and more costly than Transit Gateway.

x.A: A Savings Plan commits you to paying for usage all day, but the jobs run only 6 hours each night, so you'd pay for unused commitment.
x.B: A Reserved Instance also bills 24 hours a day, but the jobs only run about 6 hours.
x.C: The jobs can be retried on another instance if one fails, so they tolerate interruptions. Spot Instances give the largest discount for this fault-tolerant nightly work.
x.D: Larger instances cost more and don't reduce cost.

x.A: Uploading through the application servers makes them a bottleneck, so it doesn't scale well for spikes.
x.B: A Storage Gateway file gateway is for on-premises use and isn't an upload endpoint for browsers.
x.C: Presigned URLs let browsers upload straight to S3, which scales without limit and takes the upload traffic off the application servers.
x.D: Browsers can't upload directly to an EFS file system.

x.A: DynamoDB global tables are multi-Region active-active and the application would need to be converted, and the requirement is a single primary database.
x.B: Aurora MySQL with Aurora read replicas in each Region keeps one primary reservation database with Regional read endpoints, and cross-Region replication lag is typically under a second. It's globally consistent through the single primary.
x.C: RDS MySQL cross-Region read replicas replicate asynchronously with more lag, so they can't meet the under 1 second requirement as reliably.
x.D: Separate Aurora Serverless databases synchronized by Lambda isn't a single primary database and is complex and error-prone.

x.A: Copying the images on demand is manual and doesn't automate protection against disasters.
x.B: A Data Lifecycle Manager policy that creates AMIs by tag twice a day and copies them automatically to us-west-2 meets the 24 hour data loss limit with automation.
x.C: A custom Lambda function to copy backups is extra code to build and maintain.
x.D: AWS Backup with a plan based on tags, a copy destination of us-west-2, and a twice daily schedule automates backups and cross-Region copies with little effort.
x.E: Copying on demand is manual, so backups aren't automatically available in the second Region.

x.A: Security groups only have allow rules, so you can't add a deny rule to them.
x.B: Network ACLs support deny rules. Adding an inbound deny rule for the offending IP addresses on the web tier subnets blocks them quickly while the company investigates.
x.C: Security groups can't deny, and the application tier isn't where the internet traffic enters.
x.D: The application tier is in private subnets and doesn't see the illegitimate requests directly, because they reach the ALB in the public subnets.

x.A: A security group rule can't reference IP addresses from the other Region's security group in this way, and the rule needs to be on the database side.
x.B: Cross-Region VPC peering supports security group references only within the same Region, so referencing the eu-west-1 security group ID from ap-southeast-2 doesn't work.
x.C: An inter-Region VPC peering connection with updated routes, and an inbound rule on the database security group that allows the application servers' IP addresses, works. Inter-Region peering doesn't support security group references, so IP-based rules are needed.
x.D: The security group reference doesn't work across Regions, and a transit gateway design is more than needed.

x.A: A provisioned Aurora PostgreSQL cluster for each environment runs and bills all day even though each is used only about 4 hours.
x.B: RDS Single-AZ instances run and bill all day, and are used only half the time.
x.C: Aurora Serverless (on-demand, PostgreSQL-compatible) scales capacity with use and can pause when idle, so you pay only while the environment is used.
x.D: S3 with Object Select isn't a PostgreSQL database.

x.A: Config can find untagged resources, and tagging them programmatically lets the backup plan select all resources by tag, with little ongoing work.
x.B: Config identifies resource configurations, and adding resources to a vault isn't how backups are assigned. Vaults store backups.
x.C: Asking each account owner to review their resources is manual, slow, and error-prone.
x.D: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities and doesn't identify resources to back up.

x.A: S3 hosts the website, and Lambda functions resize the images when they are uploaded. All parts are serverless, highly available, and scale automatically with unpredictable traffic.
x.B: CloudFront doesn't host a website by itself and doesn't invoke Step Functions, and RDS isn't a good place to store images.
x.C: A single EC2 instance isn't highly available or scalable.
x.D: ECS with SQS and an EC2 image-resizing program still includes a server to manage and scale, so it's less scalable and takes more effort.

x.A: The node role permissions matter for node registration, but the stated problem is that the control plane is reachable only privately, so the nodes need a private path.
x.B: With public access disabled and the nodes in private subnets, the nodes need private connectivity to the control plane, so interface VPC endpoints for the needed services allow them to join the cluster.
x.C: Moving nodes to public subnets goes against the security compliance requirement.
x.D: The issue isn't blocked outbound traffic in the security group, but the lack of a private path to the control plane and related services.

x.A: Redshift supports the Data API, which lets traditional, containerized, and event-driven applications access data over HTTPS without managing connections.
x.B: Redshift supports client-side and server-side encryption of data.
x.C: Redshift fits analytics workloads that run during specified hours, such as when the application isn't active, and it can pause and resume.
x.D: Caching to reduce pressure on a backend database is a job for a cache like ElastiCache, not Redshift.
x.E: Handling tens of millions of requests per minute is a job for databases like DynamoDB, not Redshift, which is built for analytics.
x.F: Creating a secondary replica of a cluster isn't a Redshift use case in this sense.

x.A: ECS with an ALB means managing a container platform and tuning scaling, which is more operational work.
x.B: API Gateway with Lambda provisioned concurrency keeps functions warm and ready, so responses are consistently low latency during peaks, and there are no servers to manage.
x.C: EKS with an ALB is the most operational work of the options.
x.D: Reserved concurrency limits and guarantees how many instances can run, but doesn't keep them warm, so cold starts can still add latency.

x.A: Session Manager has a built-in option to send session logs to an S3 bucket, which you enable in Preferences. It's the simplest option.
x.B: Installing the CloudWatch agent and exporting logs is extra setup and manual exports.
x.C: A custom document run daily by EventBridge is custom work and isn't a continuous log of sessions.
x.D: The CloudWatch agent, a subscription, and Firehose add several components when the console option sends logs to S3 directly.

x.A: RDS storage autoscaling increases storage automatically as space runs low, with no downtime and no effort once enabled.
x.B: Increasing the instance size changes compute and memory, not disk space, and it can cause downtime.
x.C: Changing to Provisioned IOPS storage changes performance, not capacity, and it takes effort.
x.D: Backing up, restoring, and moving to a new instance causes downtime and a lot of work.

x.A: CloudFormation templates deploy infrastructure, but there's no central catalog or self-service controls, so customers would manage the templates themselves.
x.B: Service Catalog lets you centrally manage products, such as CloudFormation-based solutions, and customers deploy them through a self-service portal with controlled permissions.
x.C: Systems Manager templates (documents) automate operations tasks and aren't a self-service product catalog.
x.D: Config items record resource configuration and aren't deployable solutions.

x.A: Provisioned capacity with auto scaling can lag behind unpredictable sudden traffic, and you pay for provisioned capacity even when it isn't used.
x.B: On-demand mode scales instantly with unpredictable traffic and charges per request. With the Standard table class, it fits moderate to high throughput cost-effectively.
x.C: Standard-IA lowers storage cost for rarely accessed data but raises throughput costs, and provisioned capacity doesn't track unpredictable traffic.
x.D: Standard-IA raises per-request costs, which isn't cost-effective for moderate to high throughput.

x.A: DynamoDB doesn't integrate with Secrets Manager for authentication this way, and secrets aren't how AWS API access is authenticated.
x.B: IAM users with long-term access keys in every account have to be rotated manually, which is less secure.
x.C: Cross-account roles: each business account has a role with DynamoDB access that trusts a specific role in the inventory account. The application assumes the role with temporary credentials, which is the most secure.
x.D: DynamoDB doesn't authenticate with ACM certificates.

x.A: A Lambda function to resize the cluster is custom code to build and maintain.
x.B: The Metrics Server provides resource metrics that the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler uses to scale the number of pods with the workload.
x.C: The Cluster Autoscaler adds and removes nodes in the cluster based on pod demand, so the cluster scales in and out.
x.D: API Gateway connecting to EKS doesn't scale the cluster.
x.E: App Mesh gives observability for service networking and doesn't scale the cluster.

x.A: AppSync pipeline resolvers can combine data sources, but they need a GraphQL API and design work, and they query the tables with the application's load.
x.B: CloudFront with Lambda@Edge doesn't query multiple DynamoDB tables in this way.
x.C: API Gateway with Lambda needs code to query the tables, and the queries consume read capacity on the tables.
x.D: Athena Federated Query with the DynamoDB connector queries multiple tables with SQL through a managed connector with no code, so it's the most operationally efficient. It doesn't need extra application code.

x.A: Glue with custom scripts means writing and maintaining code, which is more effort.
x.B: AWS Batch with custom scripts also requires code and compute to run it.
x.C: Athena can query CloudTrail logs in S3 with SQL, so you can search for errors like AccessDenied and Unauthorized with no infrastructure and little effort.
x.D: QuickSight needs a data source set up first and is for dashboards, not ad hoc troubleshooting queries, so it takes more effort.

x.A: The Cost Explorer API gives programmatic access to current cost data and forecasts for the next 12 months. It needs no manual steps once integrated.
x.B: Downloading .csv files isn't programmatic access and requires manual handling.
x.C: Budgets actions can't send usage cost data through FTP, so this isn't an available feature.
x.D: Budgets reports sent by email aren't programmatic access, and they don't give the forecast data in a usable form.
